Chronology 2 — The Fall and the Origin of Sin

This is the single most consequential divergence in the whole study: the same garden scene yields opposite anthropologies, and from that fork everything downstream (atonement, the cross, salvation at the end) follows by logical necessity.

The Bible's text

  • Gen 3: the serpent, the eating, the expulsion.
  • The NT builds the doctrine of inherited sin: "through one man sin entered the world… death spread to all" (Rom 5:12–19); "in sin did my mother conceive me" (Ps 51:5). Humanity inherits a corrupted nature and stands in need of redemption it cannot self-supply.
  • Eve is "deceived" first (1 Tim 2:14); Adam's act is the federal one.

The Qur'an's text

  • Adam and his spouse are both tempted by Shaytan/Iblis, both eat (Q 7:19–25; 20:120–122). The blame is shared; there is no "Eve caused it" framing.
  • Crucially: "Then Adam received words from his Lord, and He accepted his repentance" (Q 2:37). The lapse is forgiven on the spot.
  • No original sin, no inherited guilt: "no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another" (Q 35:18; 6:164; 53:38). Each soul is born in fitra (an upright primordial nature) and is accountable only for its own deeds.
  • The descent to earth is presented within the plan announced beforehand — Adam as khalifa (Q 2:30).

Collision

QuestionBibleQur'an
Is guilt inherited?Yes (original sin)No (Q 35:18)
Is human nature corrupted by the Fall?YesNo (fitra intact)
Was the first sin immediately forgiven?No — sets up redemptionYes (Q 2:37)
Is a redeemer therefore required?YesNo
Is Eve singled out?Comparatively yesNo — shared

This is not an emphasis difference. It is a binary fork. Original sin is the reason Christianity needs a cross; its absence is why Islam needs none — exactly the forgiveness-mechanism split already isolated in cap. 09 §2.4.

Logic

  • The Islamic principle "no one bears another's burden" is both a text and a clean ethical axiom — it matches the common moral intuition that guilt is not transferable.
  • The Christian reply: original sin is usually framed (in the more defensible models) as inherited corruption/mortality, not imputed personal guilt — answering the ethical objection — and it has explanatory power for the empirically observable universality of human wrongdoing.
  • Both are internally coherent; they answer different questions (Islam: is transferred guilt just? — no; Christianity: why is everyone, in fact, a sinner? — inherited corruption).

Arbiter verdict — the Fall

Present. Same narrative skeleton (couple, tempter, transgression, consequence); opposite doctrines of what it did to humanity.

Weigh.

  • Strong (Islam, textual + ethical): Q 35:18's non-transfer of guilt is explicit and ethically intuitive; immediate forgiveness (Q 2:37) is explicit.
  • Strong (Christianity, explanatory): original sin (as corrupted nature) accounts for universal moral failure and grounds the entire redemptive arc.
  • Decisive structural fact: this fork necessitates every later divergence about atonement and salvation. It is the headwater of the seam.

Judge. On ethical parsimony of the guilt question: advantage Qur'an — non-transferable guilt is both its plain text and the stronger stand-alone moral principle. On explanatory scope for the human condition: advantage Bible — it offers a reason why all sin, which the Qur'an does not attempt. Which job a true revelation "should" do — deliver a clean ethic or explain the empirical fact of sin — is the non-arbitrable value premise. What is not in doubt: from here, the two systems are logically committed to diverge all the way to the end.
